entries.meaning: Trijata, a discerning demoness devoted to Rama's feet, tells the others her dream and urges them to serve Sita. A monkey burns Lanka and destroys its army; Ravana, naked, shaven, mutilated, and riding a donkey, goes south, while Vibhishana gains Lanka. Rama's victory is proclaimed and he summons Sita. Trijata insists the dream will come true within days. Terrified, the demonesses fall at Sita's feet and leave; Sita then despairs that the wicked Ravana will kill her when the month ends.

Sita begs Trijata, her companion in distress, to build and light a pyre so unbearable separation may end. Trijata consoles her with Rama's power and fame, then explains that fire cannot be found at night and leaves. Sita laments that neither heavenly embers, stars, nor the fire-filled moon will descend; she asks the Ashoka tree to justify its name by ending her sorrow with flame-like new leaves. Seeing her extremity, Hanuman drops Rama's ring; Sita joyfully takes it as though the Ashoka had released an ember.

Sita sees the beautiful ring inscribed with Rama's name and recognizes it, torn between joy and alarm: no one can conquer invincible Rama, nor can illusion fabricate such a ring. As she wonders, Hanuman sweetly recounts Rama's virtues and story, dispelling her grief. Invited to appear, he approaches and swears by compassionate Rama that he is Rama's messenger. He says Rama sent the ring as a token and explains how humans and monkeys became allied. His loving words convince Sita in mind, action, and speech that he serves the ocean of compassion.

Recognizing a devotee of Hari, Sita's love deepens and tears and horripilation arise. She calls Hanuman a boat for one drowning in separation and asks whether Rama and Lakshmana are well, why tender-hearted Rama has grown hard toward her, whether he remembers her, and when her eyes will again see his gentle dark body. Speech fails as she fears Rama has wholly forgotten her. Hanuman gently replies that Rama and Lakshmana are well but grieve at her grief; Rama's love for her is twice hers for him. Beginning Rama's message, Hanuman himself chokes with tears.

Rama's message says that in Sita's absence everything has reversed: tender shoots burn like fire; night is death-night, moon is sun, lotus groves are forests of spears, clouds rain boiling oil, former friends cause pain, and the threefold breeze is like a serpent's breath. Speaking might lessen grief, but no one understands. Only Rama's mind knows the essence of their love—and that mind always remains beside Sita. Hearing this, Sita loses bodily awareness in love. Hanuman urges courage: remember Rama, know his sovereignty, and see demons as moths before the fire of his arrows.

Hanuman says Rama would not delay if he knew Sita's whereabouts: the rising sun of Rama's arrows would scatter the demon-darkness. Hanuman could carry her away immediately, but lacks Rama's command. He asks her to wait a few days for Rama to come with the monkeys, kill the demons, and carry her home amid praise through the three worlds. Sita doubts that other monkeys can face mighty demons. Hanuman reveals his vast golden, mountain-like, battle-terrible form, then shrinks again and explains that monkeys possess no great strength or intellect by themselves: through the Lord's power even a tiny snake can swallow Garuda.

Sita is satisfied by Hanuman's speech, steeped in devotion, majesty, brilliance, and strength. Knowing him dear to Rama, she blesses him to become a treasury of strength and character, ageless, immortal, and rich in virtue, and asks Rama to show him abundant affection. Hanuman is overwhelmed with love; bowing repeatedly, he says her renowned, unfailing blessing has fulfilled him. Hungry at the sight of fruit, he asks permission to eat despite formidable demon guards. Sita, confident in his wisdom and strength, sends him to eat sweet fruit with Rama's feet held in his heart.

After bowing, Hanuman enters the garden, eats fruit, and uproots trees. He kills some guards; survivors report that a huge monkey has devastated the Ashoka grove, eaten fruit, uprooted trees, and crushed its defenders. Ravana sends successive warriors, whom Hanuman destroys while roaring. Aksha Kumara advances with a vast force; Hanuman fells him with a tree and kills, crushes, or grinds his soldiers into dust. Survivors report the monkey's immense power.

Enraged by his son's death, Ravana sends powerful Meghanada with orders not to kill but bind the monkey and discover his origin. Indrajit arrives furious over his brother's death. Hanuman uproots a vast tree, smashes his chariot, and crushes the accompanying warriors. The two clash like elephant-kings; Hanuman's fist briefly stuns Indrajit. Unable to defeat the Wind's son even through illusion, Indrajit invokes Brahma's weapon. Hanuman decides that refusing honour to the Brahmastra would diminish its immeasurable glory.

Indrajit strikes Hanuman with Brahma's missile. Even while falling, Hanuman destroys a troop, then feigns unconsciousness and permits himself to be bound with serpent-nooses and carried away for Rama's purpose. Shiva notes that wise people sever worldly bondage by repeating the name of Hanuman's Lord—how could that Lord's messenger truly be bound? Demons crowd Ravana's splendid court. Hanuman sees gods and guardians of directions standing humbly in fear, yet remains as fearless as Garuda among serpents. Ravana laughs and abuses him, but memory of his son's death brings grief.
